body: Peak/trough: the Sensex rose from ~1,000 in early 1991 and ~2,000 in Jan 1992 to 4,467 in April 1992 (the Feb 1992 liberalisation budget added fuel), then fell to ~2,529 by Aug 1992 and below ~2,000 by spring 1993 - roughly a 55% drawdown (trough level approximate). Mechanism: Harshad Mehta used bank-to-bank 'ready forward' deals and bank receipts (BRs) that were not backed by securities to channel bank money into stocks; banks were left holding fake BRs (~Rs 4,000 crore owed per one source; totals of Rs 5,000 crore and higher are also cited). Exposed by Sucheta Dalal in the Times of India on 23 Apr 1992. What led: a narrow set of 'operator' stocks - ACC went from ~Rs 200 to ~Rs 9,000 in about three months (~4,400%); what lagged/collapsed afterwards: the same names, plus banks hit by the BR losses. Valuation at peak: Sensex P/E was reportedly ~50x+ (unverified). Top signals visible at the time: parabolic moves in a few stocks without earnings support, a celebrity broker ('Big Bull'), unexplained liquidity, and front-page euphoria. Aftermath: SEBI got statutory powers (1992), NSE screen trading began (1994). Lesson: when a rally is financed by leverage nobody can trace, the size of the eventual fall depends on the source of funding, not on fundamentals.

data.early_signals: operator stocks parabolic, untraceable bank funding

title: Harshad Mehta bull run and bust (1991-93)
